cls: Beta-1 selective (cardioselective) adrenergic blocker - ultra-short-acting IV
pharm: Competitively blocks beta-1 adrenergic receptors, slowing the sinus rate and AV-nodal conduction and lowering heart rate and blood pressure; its very short duration of action allows minute-to-minute IV titration
quick: Optional 500 mcg/kg load over 1 min, then 50 mcg/kg/min IV, titrate every 4 min to max 200 mcg/kg/min (300 for hypertension)
Not applicable - given only by IV infusion
Use only if clearly needed; can cause fetal bradycardia/hypoglycaemia
Unknown if excreted in milk; use caution, short half-life favours minimal exposure
Acid metabolite accumulates in renal impairment; use caution and monitor
Metabolised by RBC esterases, not the liver; no specific adjustment
Not relevant for short-term IV use
Continuous ECG, blood pressure, heart rate and IV site (extravasation)
summary: Esmolol is an ultra-short-acting, beta-1 selective adrenergic blocker given only by IV infusion for the short-term control of ventricular rate in supraventricular tachycardia (including atrial fibrillation/flutter) and noncompensatory sinus tachycardia, and for tachycardia and hypertension during the perioperative period. An optional loading dose of 500 mcg/kg over 1 minute is followed by 50 mcg/kg/min, titrated upward every 4 minutes (extra loading doses optional) to a maximum maintenance of 200 mcg/kg/min for tachycardia or 250-300 mcg/kg/min for hypertension. It is hydrolysed by red-cell esterases, giving a distribution half-life of about 2 minutes and an elimination half-life of about 9 minutes, so its effects dissipate within ~10-20 minutes of stopping the infusion - ideal for minute-to-minute titration. Hypotension is the most common adverse effect. Maintenance infusions are intended for up to 48 hours.
indications: Rapid control of ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter in perioperative, postoperative or other emergent settings
Noncompensatory sinus tachycardia where rapid heart rate requires intervention
Short-term treatment of tachycardia and hypertension occurring during induction/intubation, surgery, emergence from anaesthesia and the postoperative period

dosage.d: Optional 500 mcg/kg loading over 1 min, then 50 mcg/kg/min for 4 min; step-wise repeat optional load and increase by 50 mcg/kg/min every 4 min to max 200 mcg/kg/min
dosage.n: Effective maintenance 50-200 mcg/kg/min; >200 adds little rate effect and more adverse reactions

dosage.d: 500 mcg/kg over 1 min, then 50 mcg/kg/min for 4 min; continue as for SVT
dosage.n: Titrate to heart rate and blood pressure

dosage.d: 1 mg/kg bolus over 30 sec, then 150 mcg/kg/min if needed; titrate to max 200 (tachycardia) or 300 (hypertension) mcg/kg/min
dosage.n: Safety of doses above 300 mcg/kg/min not studied

dosage.d: 30 min after first dose of the alternative drug, halve the esmolol rate; after the second dose, discontinue if control maintained for 1 hour

admin: For intravenous use only; administer by continuous infusion, preferably via an infusion pump
Titrate against ventricular rate or blood pressure at intervals of at least 4 minutes
Avoid small veins or butterfly catheters; infusion-site reactions and rarely necrosis can occur with extravasation
Not compatible with 5% sodium bicarbonate (limited stability) or furosemide (precipitation)
Limit maintenance infusions to up to 48 hours
Monitor blood pressure and ECG continuously; hypotension is common and resolves quickly after slowing/stopping the infusion
moa: Esmolol is a competitive, beta-1 selective (cardioselective) adrenergic antagonist with no significant intrinsic sympathomimetic or membrane-stabilising activity at therapeutic doses. By blocking beta-1 receptors it reduces heart rate, slows AV-nodal conduction, lowers myocardial contractility and reduces blood pressure, thereby controlling ventricular rate in supraventricular arrhythmias and blunting perioperative sympathetic surges. It contains an ester linkage that is rapidly hydrolysed by red-blood-cell esterases to an essentially inactive acid metabolite and methanol, giving it an ultra-short half-life and allowing rapid onset and offset of effect.

absolute: Second- or third-degree AV block without a functioning pacemaker
monitor: Signs of bronchospasm in at-risk patients

preg: There are no adequate well-controlled studies in pregnant women; beta-blockers can cause fetal bradycardia, hypoglycaemia and growth restriction, and esmolol has been associated with maternal hypotension affecting the fetus. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the risk, with fetal/maternal monitoring.
lact: It is not known whether esmolol is excreted in human milk. Because of its very short half-life and IV-only short-term use, infant exposure is likely minimal, but caution is advised and monitoring of a breastfed infant for bradycardia/hypoglycaemia is reasonable.
renal: The acid metabolite of esmolol is eliminated renally and can accumulate (about 10-fold) in patients with end-stage renal disease, though the parent drug's clearance is unchanged. Use with caution and monitor in renal impairment.
hepatic: Esmolol is metabolised by red-blood-cell esterases rather than hepatic enzymes, so hepatic impairment is not expected to materially alter its clearance; no specific dose adjustment is recommended.

major: Verapamil/diltiazem and other rate-slowing drugs - additive bradycardia, AV block and hypotension; avoid in patients with poor cardiac function
moderate: Digoxin - esmolol may raise digoxin levels; additive AV-nodal slowing
Clonidine - risk of rebound hypertension if clonidine withdrawn while on a beta-blocker
minor: Morphine - increases steady-state esmolol levels modestly
Neuromuscular blockers - esmolol may prolong their action
interactions.alcohol: Not relevant for short-term IV use
interactions.diagnostics: May mask tachycardia that would otherwise signal hypoglycaemia or hyperthyroidism; affects heart rate/blood pressure readings

common: Hypotension (symptomatic and asymptomatic) - the most frequent effect
serious: Severe hypotension that may be life-threatening
Marked bradycardia, AV block or asystole
rare: Metabolic acidosis with high-dose/prolonged use (methanol/acid metabolite)
emergency: Symptomatic severe bradycardia or high-grade AV block

monitoring: Continuous ECG for rate, rhythm and conduction
Blood pressure frequently or continuously during titration
Heart rate as the titration endpoint
IV infusion site for extravasation or local reaction
Respiratory status in patients with reactive airway disease
Blood glucose in diabetics (masking of hypoglycaemia symptoms)
counsel: This is a fast-acting heart-rate-lowering medicine given only by a drip in hospital under close monitoring
Tell staff at once if you feel faint, very dizzy, short of breath or have pain at the drip site
Its effects wear off quickly once the drip is slowed or stopped
If you have asthma, diabetes or heart problems, make sure the team knows
You will be watched on a heart monitor while receiving it
pk: Beta-blockade within about 1-2 minutes (faster with loading dose)
Steady-state plasma levels in about 30 minutes without a loading dose (about 5 minutes with loading)
Distribution about 2 minutes; elimination about 9 minutes
Effects largely dissipate within 10-20 minutes of stopping the infusion
Store at controlled room temperature; protect from freezing; use diluted solutions per product labelling
pearls: Ultra-short-acting: hydrolysed by RBC esterases (not liver/kidney), elimination half-life ~9 min - ideal for minute-to-minute titration
Hypotension is the dominant adverse effect and resolves rapidly when the infusion is slowed or stopped
Titrate no faster than every 4 minutes; doses >200 mcg/kg/min add little rate control but more adverse effects
Limit maintenance infusions to ~48 hours; transition to a longer-acting agent by halving the rate 30 min after the first oral dose
Incompatible with sodium bicarbonate and furosemide; avoid extravasation (risk of skin necrosis)
missed: Not applicable - esmolol is administered only as a controlled IV infusion in a monitored setting, not as scheduled self-administered doses.
overdose: Overdose causes severe bradycardia, hypotension, AV block, cardiogenic shock and bronchospasm; because of the ~9-minute half-life, simply stopping the infusion usually leads to rapid improvement. If treatment is needed: IV atropine or temporary pacing for bradycardia, IV fluids and vasopressors for hypotension, glucagon and/or beta-agonists for refractory cases, and a beta-2 agonist for bronchospasm. Manage in a monitored setting.
